topics.label: Lecture introduction and learning objectives
topics.groupedBecause: The lecturer introduces the course context, outlines the main lecture goals, and sets up the central question of what causes cancer.

topics.label: Cancer development and the balance of genetics, environment, and chance
topics.groupedBecause: These subtopics examine how cancer arises from genetic mutations and microenvironmental factors, contrasting intrinsic bad luck with external exposures and global epidemiological variation.

topics.label: Infectious agents and viral mechanisms in cancer
topics.groupedBecause: These subtopics explain how pathogens such as viruses and bacteria contribute to malignancy, detailing the specific etiology and mechanisms of Burkitt lymphoma.

topics.label: Mechanisms of chemical and radiation-induced DNA damage
topics.groupedBecause: These subtopics detail how environmental agents, dietary toxins, and radiation directly or metabolically modify DNA to produce mutagenic damage.

topics.label: Tumor promotion, host susceptibility, and mechanisms of carcinogenesis
topics.groupedBecause: These subtopics contrast mutational initiation with promotional processes like chronic inflammation and highlight how host tissue state and life stages influence malignant transformation.

topics.label: Methodologies for identifying and testing carcinogenicity
topics.groupedBecause: These subtopics describe experimental, epidemiological, and genomic approaches used to detect mutagenic signatures and establish whether exposures cause cancer.

topics.label: Lecture summary and risk-benefit considerations
topics.groupedBecause: The lecturer concludes the lecture by weighing environmental risks against daily benefits and summarizing the challenges of establishing carcinogenicity.
